title: Boaz Was Closer to David Than Most People Realize — And His Family Story Points Straight to Jesus
paragraphs: Boaz Was Closer to David Than Most People Realize — And His Family Story Points Straight to Jesus

He was not merely a distant ancestor in an old genealogy. Boaz was King David’s great-grandfather—and when you follow the bloodline through Ruth, Rahab, David, and ultimately Jesus Christ, you discover something breathtaking about the kind of families God is willing to redeem.
There is a detail hidden near the end of Ruth that is easy to read too quickly.
A wedding happens.
A child is born.
Names are recorded.
The story appears to be ending.
But then Scripture quietly drops a name that changes the meaning of everything that came before it.
David.
Not just any David.
The David.
The shepherd boy.
The giant killer.
The psalmist.
The fugitive.
The warrior.
The sinner who would fall catastrophically.
The repentant king.
The man whose royal line would eventually lead the Gospel writer Matthew to Jesus Christ.
And suddenly you realize that the little love story between a grieving Moabite widow and an honorable man from Bethlehem was never merely about two lonely people finding each other.
God was building a royal family while almost everyone involved was simply trying to survive.
That should make some of us stop reading for a moment.
Because perhaps you have looked at the broken pieces of your own family and wondered whether anything beautiful could possibly come from them.
Perhaps there are names in your family history you would rather not discuss.
Divorce.
Addiction.
Abandonment.
Betrayal.
Infidelity.
Poverty.
Abuse.
Prison.
Failure.
Secrets.
Maybe your family tree does not look like something God would use.
Neither did this one.
And that is exactly why you need to understand who Boaz was to David.
The Hebrew text at the end of Ruth gives the genealogy with almost startling simplicity:
וְשַׂלְמוֹן֙ הוֹלִ֣יד אֶת־בֹּ֔עַז וּבֹ֖עַז הוֹלִ֥יד אֶת־עוֹבֵֽד׃ וְעֹבֵד֙ הוֹלִ֣יד אֶת־יִשָׁ֔י וְיִשַׁ֖י הוֹלִ֥יד אֶת־דָּוִֽד׃
Ve-Salmon holid et-Bo'az, u-Vo'az holid et-Oved; ve-Oved holid et-Yishai, ve-Yishai holid et-David.
In straightforward English:
Salmon fathered Boaz. Boaz fathered Obed. Obed fathered Jesse. Jesse fathered David.
That genealogy is explicitly preserved in Ruth 4:21–22.
So how exactly was Boaz related to David?
Boaz was David's great-grandfather.
Boaz and Ruth became the parents of Obed.
Obed became the father of Jesse.
Jesse became the father of David.
Boaz → Obed → Jesse → David.
There is no need to speculate. Scripture gives us the relationship directly.
But knowing the answer is only the beginning.
Because once you know who Boaz was to David, another question becomes far more interesting:
Why did God make sure we knew?
Ruth begins nowhere near a throne.
It begins with famine.
A man named Elimelech leaves Bethlehem with his wife Naomi and their sons. They settle in Moab. Then Elimelech dies. Naomi's sons marry Moabite women, Ruth and Orpah.
Then both sons die too.
Three widows.
Three funerals.
No obvious future.
No king.
No palace.
No heroic music playing in the background.
Just grief.
Naomi eventually returns to Bethlehem so devastated that she tells the women there not to call her Naomi—associated with pleasantness—but Mara, meaning bitter.
She had left full, she said, and returned empty.
And somewhere reading this is a person who understands that sentence without needing it explained.
You left one season believing life was going somewhere.
Then the phone rang.
The relationship ended.
The person died.
The money disappeared.
The betrayal surfaced.
The prayer seemed unanswered.
The future you had pictured collapsed.
You came back carrying a version of yourself you barely recognized.
Naomi believed she had returned empty.
But walking beside her was Ruth.
And Naomi could not yet see what God was going to do through the woman walking beside her.
That is one of the brutal limitations of pain:
grief can make emptiness feel more visible than grace.
Ruth was a Moabite outsider. Humanly speaking, she did not arrive in Bethlehem looking like the beginning of a royal dynasty.
She arrived as a widow gathering leftover grain.
Think about that.
The great-grandmother of King David entered this part of the biblical story picking up what harvesters left behind.
And then she walked into the field of Boaz.
Boaz is introduced as a man of standing from Elimelech's family. As Ruth's story unfolds, he becomes the willing family redeemer who acts lawfully and compassionately toward Ruth and Naomi.
This matters because the biblical idea surrounding redemption in Ruth is not sentimental romance.
It involves costly covenant responsibility.
The Hebrew root associated with the redeemer is גאל — ga'al, and the related noun גֹּאֵל — go'el refers to one who acts as a redeemer within the obligations of kinship.
Boaz does not merely tell Ruth that he cares.
He acts.
He protects.
He provides.
He assumes responsibility.
He publicly settles the matter at the city gate.
He pays the cost associated with taking up the family obligation.
And then he marries Ruth.
Scripture says that the LORD enabled Ruth to conceive, and she gave birth to a son.
They called him Obed.
Then Scripture pulls the camera backward.
Obed becomes the father of Jesse.
Jesse becomes the father of David.
The grieving widow gathering grain in a Bethlehem field becomes the great-grandmother of Israel's most famous king.
And Boaz becomes David's great-grandfather.
But centuries later, another genealogy opens.
Matthew begins tracing the ancestry of Jesus Christ.
Genealogies are the part many readers are tempted to skim.
Do not skim this one.
Because suddenly familiar names appear.
Matthew records that Salmon fathered Boaz by Rahab, Boaz fathered Obed by Ruth, Obed fathered Jesse, and Jesse fathered David the king.
Read that again slowly.
Rahab.
Ruth.
Boaz.
Obed.
Jesse.
David.
And Matthew keeps going.
Toward Jesus.

This does not mean every detail people sometimes attach to these characters is equally certain. We should be careful not to turn speculation into Scripture. But Matthew explicitly names Rahab in connection with Boaz and Ruth in connection with Obed. That claim is in the biblical text itself.
And now the family tree becomes almost unbearably beautiful.
Rahab's story begins for us in Jericho, where she is identified as a prostitute.
Ruth is a Moabite widow.
David becomes Israel's celebrated king—but later commits adultery with Bathsheba and orchestrates Uriah's death.
Yet the genealogy keeps moving.
Not because sin does not matter.
It matters so much that Christ had to die.
Not because repentance is optional.
Jesus' message calls sinners to turn to God.
Not because grace pretends evil never happened.
Grace is not denial.
Grace is God's undeserved mercy toward guilty and broken people, ultimately displayed at the cross where Christ bore sin and opened the way of reconciliation to God.
That distinction matters.
The message of this genealogy is not, “Your past doesn't matter.”
The message is far more powerful:
Your past does not have greater authority than the redeeming purposes of God.
There are consequences God does not erase.
There are wounds that leave scars.
There are choices that cannot simply be undone.
David himself would learn that painfully.
Christian redemption is not God calling darkness light.
It is God entering our darkness with a Savior.
And this is where Boaz becomes more than an interesting answer to a Bible trivia question.
Boaz was a real redeemer within the historical and covenant setting of Ruth.
But Christians should not confuse Boaz with Jesus or force every detail of his life into an allegory. Boaz is not Christ.
Jesus is infinitely greater.
Yet the biblical theme of redemption that shines through Ruth prepares our hearts to understand something central to the Gospel:
redemption costs the redeemer something.
Boaz was willing to act for Ruth.
Jesus came to save sinners at the cost of His own blood.
Peter writes that believers were redeemed not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ.
That is the center.
Not Boaz.
Not David.
Not Ruth.
Not Rahab.
Jesus.
Boaz's story moves toward David.
David's royal line moves toward Christ.

Matthew intentionally presents Jesus as the Messiah, the son of David, the son of Abraham, and organizes the genealogy around the movement from Abraham to David, David to the exile, and the exile to the Christ.
And there is something especially moving about Bethlehem.
Ruth gathered grain around Bethlehem.
Boaz lived there.
Obed entered the family story there.
David would come from Bethlehem.
And generations later, according to the Gospel accounts, Jesus would be born in Bethlehem.
The field that looked ordinary was standing inside a story far larger than anyone could see.
Maybe your life feels like that field right now.
Ordinary.
Unnoticed.
Hard.
You are simply trying to make it through another day.
Trying to raise your children.
Trying to rebuild your marriage.
Trying to resist the temptation nobody knows about.
Trying to forgive someone who wounded you.
Trying to pray when heaven feels silent.
Trying to come back to Jesus after wandering farther than you ever intended.
You may think nothing significant is happening.
Ruth probably did not wake up every morning thinking, “I am becoming the great-grandmother of a king.”
She needed food.
Naomi needed hope.
Boaz needed to decide whether he would live honorably before God.
They lived faithfully inside the day they had been given.
God could see generations they could not.
That does not mean every Christian will become famous, wealthy, influential, or historically remembered. Scripture never promises that.
Something better is true.
No act of faithfulness offered to Christ is meaningless simply because nobody applauds it.
You do not know what God may accomplish through an obedient decision made when nobody is watching.
The prayer you pray with your child.
The temptation you finally confess.
The relationship you refuse to compromise.
The person you forgive.
The Bible you open again after months away.
The church you return to.
The apology you finally make.
The secret sin you drag into the light.
The Gospel you share with one frightened person.
The decision to follow Jesus when your emotions are screaming for you to walk away.
You see today.
God sees generations.
And maybe that is why this genealogy hurts in the best possible way.
Because some of us have spent years believing our family history disqualified us.
“My father wasn't there.”
“My mother failed me.”
“My marriage collapsed.”
“I destroyed years of my life.”
“My children have seen things I wish they had never seen.”
“I have sexual sin in my past.”
“I've been addicted.”
“I've lied.”
“I've cheated.”
“I've walked away from God.”
“I knew better and still did it.”
Listen carefully.
The genealogy of Jesus does not give us permission to romanticize sin.
It gives sinners permission to run toward the Savior.
The cross does not say sin was insignificant.
The cross shows exactly how serious sin is.
The Son of God gave Himself for sinners.
And the resurrection announces that sin and death do not get the final word over those who belong to Christ.
This is why Christianity is not self-improvement.
You do not need a slightly cleaner version of yourself.
You need redemption.
You need forgiveness.
You need reconciliation with God.
You need the righteousness you cannot manufacture.
You need Jesus Christ.
Maybe you have been trying to edit your reputation while Jesus is calling you to surrender your heart.
Stop hiding.
Come into the light.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the failure.
Bring Him the years you cannot recover.
Bring Him the family history you cannot rewrite.
You cannot change yesterday.
But Jesus can redeem the person who lived it.
That is grace.
And grace changes what happens next.
That is why the journey from Boaz to David matters.
Boaz did not live long enough to see everything God would accomplish through his descendants.
He never saw David standing before Goliath.
He never heard David's psalms echo through generations.
He never watched kings rise from that family line.
He never stood in Bethlehem centuries later and saw Mary holding the infant Jesus.
Boaz simply lived faithfully in his generation.
And God wrote his faithfulness into a story that reached far beyond his lifetime.
What if obedience is more important than visibility?
What if faithfulness matters more than applause?
What if the decision you make with Jesus tonight matters beyond what you can presently measure?
That is worth sitting with.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding from God, do not turn this into another article you read, felt, and forgot.
Talk to Him.
Be honest.
Someone reading beneath you may desperately need evidence that Jesus still restores people.

That is a meaningful way to support Gospel-centered work and glorify God: not because clicking a button earns God's favor—it absolutely does not—but because willingly helping biblical truth reach another person can be an act of Christian generosity and witness.
It does not make God love you more.
It does not earn salvation.
Salvation is by God's grace, received through faith in Christ.
But supporting Gospel-centered ministry can be one practical way of participating in work you believe is helping people hear biblical truth.
Because now you know the answer.
How was Boaz related to David?
He was David's great-grandfather.
Boaz fathered Obed.
Obed fathered Jesse.
Jesse fathered David.
But beneath that simple genealogy is something far harder to forget.
A widow thought her future was finished.
A grieving woman thought she had returned empty.
A foreigner gathered leftovers from a field.
A man quietly chose integrity.
A child named Obed was born.
Then Jesse.
Then David.
And generations later, the genealogy leads us to Jesus Christ.
The people inside the story could see only the page they were living.
God could see where the genealogy was going.
Maybe tonight you can only see your page too.
Do not confuse an unfinished chapter with a finished story.
Repent where you have sinned.
Trust Christ where you are afraid.
Obey Him where the next step is clear.
And leave the pages you cannot see in the hands of the God who already sees them.
Because sometimes the place you thought your story ended is exactly where grace begins writing a name you never expected.
